newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Honduras launches $18 billion development plan.
newsitem.headline: Honduras launches $18 billion development plan.

text.p: Honduras on Thursday launched an ambitious development plan that would require $18 billion in investment.
Among the proposals is a "dry canal" to link container ship ports on the Atlantic and Pacific with a high-speed rail. Similar plans also are being discussed in Nicaragua, Mexico and Colombia.
President Carlos Roberto Reina on Thursday signed an executive agreemment authorizing a local foundation to begin studies and seek financing for the projects.

One potential source of financing is the Interamerican Development Bank, which would be willing to provide credit to private developers, bank representative Federico Alvarez said at a ceremony announcing the plans.

The so-called Great National Transformation Project, proposed by the local private sector, was described by President Reina as something that "cannot be postponed in order to promote development and fight poverty." The plan calls for projects to be developed by the private sector, both local and international, while the government creates the macroeconomic, fiscal and legal incentives to attract capital.

Apart from the dry canal, proposals include a huge tourist, commercial and industrial zone at Trujillo and Castilla on the Atlantic Coast to be built over the next 10 years. The foundation would promote the construction of highways and airports throughout the country.

Among the proposals is to use the U.S. Army base at Palmerola in the center of the country, currently home to 500 U.S. troops, as a private air terminal. Other concessions under the plan include two large hydroelectric plants, an African palm cultivation project, new banana plantations, mine exploration and reforestation to boost the timber industry.
Corporate taxes would be lowered and import and export taxes eliminated. The Honduran constitution would be reformed to expand land-ownership rights for foreigners and privatize the pension system.

Miguel Facusse, a Honduran investor and major backer of the project, said at the unveiling ceremony that the plan could be executed in two phases over the next 10 years, with the first phase costing $6 billion and the second $12 billion.
"We're talking about a substantial change of economic and social strategy aimed at stopping poverty," Facusse said.
